name: Ivan Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a tyre and servicing garage on the main road, one of three the same owner runs. Mornings are tyres and tracking, afternoons I'm on oil services and pads, and the senior lads take the engine stuff. I like the pace, honestly, there's always a car on the ramp. What wears me out is the targets, because the owner's office counts how many services each of us does per shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does the money leave you at the end of the month?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not far. I'm on the junior rate, my girlfriend Ana is a teaching assistant, and we rent a one-bed above a takeaway. I've got maybe three weeks of money saved if both of us stopped. There's one other garage in town and they've got a waiting list for jobs, not for customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but it did tidy a few things up. The owner's booking system started sending text reminders on its own, which the customers like. Nothing else at the bench changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, the targets are the problem, not AI. The owner already tracks everything per shift, and if AI only speeds up the paperwork, he'll just expect more cars through. I'm the slowest on the team, so I'm always looking over my shoulder a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to get my numbers up, maybe ask the senior lad, Tomasz, to show me his shortcuts on pad changes. I'd also start putting twenty quid a week aside. I'd keep using the chatbot on my phone to check torque settings, because it saves me asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just aware I'm on thin ice if the numbers dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned using the chatbot. Does the owner know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd probably like it, to be fair, as long as it's right. I always double-check against the manual. A wrong torque on a wheel nut isn't a joke. The chatbot is like a quick mate to ask, not a boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if your hours got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're short on rent within a month, simple as that. Ana's pay is steady but it's not enough for both of us. We'd probably skip her sister's wedding trip in the spring, which she'd hate.

say: AI was **oversold**, though the booking system's **text reminders** helped customers.
Nothing changed at the **bench**, where the real work happens.
think: The **targets** worry me more than AI, because quicker paperwork means more cars expected.
I'm the **slowest on the team**, so I'm always slightly on edge.
do: Ask Tomasz for his **shortcuts** on pad changes to lift my numbers.
Save **twenty pounds a week** toward a small cushion.
Keep using the **phone chatbot** for torque settings, checked against the manual.
feel: **Uneasy**, aware I'm on thin ice if my numbers drop.
S0.quote: A wrong torque on a wheel nut isn't a joke. The chatbot is like a quick mate to ask, not a boss.
fieldNote: Ivan already lives with **per-shift targets**, which shape how he reads every scenario.
He uses AI casually but **double-checks** it, a careful, middle-of-the-road user.
Money is tight enough that a **family wedding trip** would be the first thing cut.

steps.text: Ask Tomasz to show his quicker method for pad changes
Put twenty pounds a week into savings
Keep checking torque settings with the phone chatbot and the manual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the owner should share the savings with the people on the floor. If the software is doing the bookings and ordering parts, that's money saved, and it shouldn't all go up to him. I'd probably say that in the group chat at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the front desk job goes. Sandra does bookings and parts at our site, and the owner already said a system could do all three sites. Then the screen tells us what to fix and the targets go up again, and the slow one gets moved on. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about getting the garage to pay for my hybrid and electric training, because those cars are coming in more and the old lads won't touch them. I'd use the AI tools more once I see Tomasz using them properly. And I'd talk to the others about joining a union together, because one of us asking gets nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's a way through, but I can see the door shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owner should share the savings. Do you think he would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on his own. That's why I'd want the union in, so it's not just me in his office. He's not a bad bloke, but he runs it on spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sandra if her job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not her fault and help her look, honestly. She's been there twelve years and knows every regular by name. A computer won't know that our regular Mr Patel's car pulls left because he hit a kerb in 2019.

say: The owner should **share the savings** from software with the people on the floor.
I'd say that openly in the **work group chat**.
think: The **front desk** job probably goes when software books and orders for all three sites.
Higher targets mean the **slowest mechanic**, which is me, gets moved on.
do: Ask the garage to fund **hybrid and electric** training this year.
Use **AI tools** more once Tomasz shows they work properly.
Get the team to **join a union** together rather than ask alone.
feel: **Anxious**, seeing a way through but feeling the door **shrink**.
S1.quote: A computer won't know that our regular Mr Patel's car pulls left because he hit a kerb in 2019.
fieldNote: Ivan expects desk work to go first, naming **Sandra on bookings** before himself.
His progressive streak comes out as wanting savings shared and a **collective voice**.
He'd adopt AI tools only **once a trusted colleague** shows they work.

steps.text: Ask the owner to pay for hybrid and electric vehicle training
Copy Tomasz's use of the diagnostic AI once he's tested it
Get the floor team to join a union together

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying this needs to be stopped or slowed down, properly, by government. And that whoever owns the robots should be taxed to pay everyone else. I'd post that and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real talk, the thinking side of my job goes in 2028: the diagnosis, the quoting, the parts lists. Then I'm just hands for three years, and they'll pay hands less. By 2031 a robot does tyres and pads, which is exactly what I do, and I'm thirty-one with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd cut everything, no takeaways, sell my car and use the bus. I'd join the union and any protest going. I'd ask the council about free courses in something with people, maybe support work, because Ana says schools will still need adults in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. Like the ground going under you while you're still standing on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell your car. You work at a garage. Isn't that hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it's daft, a mechanic with no car. But it's two hundred a month I haven't got. I'd borrow Tomasz's for anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd stick together and work it out, and that we hold off on getting a dog or anything like that. Then probably I'd lie awake doing sums. I do sums when I'm scared.

say: Government should **slow this down**, and robot owners should be **taxed** to support everyone.
I'd post that openly and **mean it**.
think: Diagnosis, quoting and parts lists go in **2028**, leaving me as cheaper hands.
By **2031** robots do tyres and pads, exactly my work, when I'm thirty-one.
do: **Sell my car** and take the bus to save two hundred a month.
**Join the union** and turn up to protests.
Ask the council about **free courses** in support work.
feel: **Scared**, like the ground going while I'm still standing on it.
S2.quote: By 2031 a robot does tyres and pads, which is exactly what I do, and I'm thirty-one with nothing.
fieldNote: Ivan reasons clearly about the **three-year gap**: thinking work goes first, then his hands-on work.
He would make a **painful sacrifice**, selling his car, despite being a mechanic.
His fallback idea of **support work** comes from his partner's school job.

steps.text: Sell his car and use the bus to work
Join the union and attend AI protests
Ask the council about free support-work courses
Post publicly calling for a tax on robot owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and get the unions and the government to plan something real. Robot owners pay, workers retrain on decent money. Same as I said with the fast one, just with less shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2034 is when the robots come for tyres and pads, so I'd be thirty-five. That's time to get qualified in something else, if I don't just drift. The quoting and diagnosis going in 2031 is the warning sign I'd watch for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the hybrid and electric course in year one, because that keeps me useful for the next five years at least. I'd start a proper savings pot, even fifty a month. And around year three I'd look seriously at a second trade, maybe as a support worker or something in schools like Ana.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but less sick about it. There's a plan I can picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd want to bring along with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, definitely. He's brilliant with an engine but he won't touch a computer. I'd drag him on the course if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that would make you drift instead of acting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The garage being busy and things seeming fine. When there's a full board you don't think about 2034. A busy garage is the trap.

say: We've got **a few years**, so unions and government should plan something real.
Robot owners should pay so workers can **retrain on decent money**.
think: Robots reach tyres and pads by **2034**, when I'll be thirty-five.
Losing **quoting and diagnosis** in 2031 is the warning sign I'd watch.
do: Take the **hybrid and electric** course in the first year.
Save **fifty pounds a month** in a separate pot.
Look seriously at a **second trade** around year three.
feel: **Anxious**, but less sick, because I can picture a plan.
S3.quote: When there's a full board you don't think about 2034. A busy garage is the trap.
fieldNote: Five years turns Ivan's fear into a **staged plan**: upskill first, second trade later.
He wants to bring **Tomasz** along, showing loyalty to colleagues.
He names his own risk clearly: a **busy garage** lulls him into drifting.

steps.text: Complete the hybrid and electric vehicle course in year one
Set up a fifty-pound monthly savings pot
Push the union for retraining paid by robot owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and the government has no excuse not to set up retraining. I'd want the unions at the table from day one. That's my public line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one I can actually live with. 2039 robots means I've got a good run in the trade, and if I'm on electric cars I'm the last one they'd replace. The worry is whether there's any work by then for someone who's only ever done this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electric course, then try for my senior grade in a few years. I'd save steady, and maybe Ana and I would finally plan a kid, around year four, once I know where I stand. I'd keep using AI for the paperwork side so it's not a stranger when it takes over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. It's a long way off, but it's still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you were selling your car. What happens to that plan here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the car in this one. Ten years, I can afford to wait and see how it goes. I'd only cut if things went the fast way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a kid. Does AI change that decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. In the fast one I wouldn't dare have a kid. With ten years, I'd think the kid's at school and I'll have figured something out.

say: Ten years is **a gift** if we use it, so government has no excuse.
Unions should be **at the table** from day one.
think: Robots in **2039** give me a good run, especially working on **electric cars**.
The open question is whether there's **any work** later for someone with only this trade.
do: Finish the **electric course** and aim for **senior grade** within a few years.
**Save steadily** and think about starting a family around year four.
Use **AI for paperwork** now so it's familiar when it takes over.
feel: **Uneasy**, since it's far off but still coming.
S4.quote: In the fast one I wouldn't dare have a kid. With ten years, I'd think the kid's at school and I'll have figured something out.
fieldNote: With a decade, Ivan's mood drops to **uneasy** and he keeps his car.
AI timing directly shapes his **family plans**, especially when to have a child.
He plans to stay in the trade by moving toward **electric cars**, the hardest work to automate.

steps.text: Finish the electric vehicle course and aim for senior grade
Save a steady amount each month
Plan with Ana to try for a child around year four
Use AI tools for job sheets and parts lists

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. That one gets my hands and my head in three years, and Ana and I have three weeks of money. What would help is a proper wage while you retrain, paid for by the people making the money from the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who aren't in the room. Sandra on the desk, Tomasz who won't touch a screen. Everyone talks about young people adapting, but the garage runs on people who won't.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about young people adapting, but the garage runs on people who won't.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** junior at a three-site tyre and servicing garage with per-shift targets.
He rents above a takeaway with Ana, a teaching assistant, and has about **three weeks** saved.
He uses AI casually, **double-checking** it, and adopts tools once colleagues prove them.
He swings from **uneasy to alarmed** with faster AGI, then plans calmly with ten years.
He wants unions at the table and **robot owners taxed** to fund retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, taking his thinking work then his hands-on work within three years.
whatWouldHelp: A **proper wage while retraining**, paid for by those profiting from robots.
